content: Progestin-only oral contraceptives are prescribed to prevent pregnancy. Progestin, a synthetic form of the female hormone progesterone, works by inhibiting ovulation (the release of eggs from the ovaries), altering the consistency of cervical mucus to make it more difficult for sperm to reach the egg, and modifying the uterine lining to prevent implantation. While these contraceptives are highly effective in preventing pregnancy, they do not offer protection against HIV/AIDS or other sexually transmitted infections. Progestin-only oral contraceptives are available in tablet form and are taken orally once daily, at the same time each day. It is essential to follow the instructions on the prescription label precisely. If you have any questions, consult your doctor or pharmacist for clarification. Do not take more or fewer pills than prescribed, and do not alter the frequency of administration. Each pack contains 28 pills, and you should begin the next pack immediately after finishing the previous one. Ideally, you should start taking the pills on the first day of your menstrual period. If you start on a different day, use an additional method of contraception, such as condoms or spermicide, for the next 48 hours. If you have experienced a miscarriage or abortion, you can begin taking the pills the following day. Progestin-only contraceptives are safe for breastfeeding mothers. If you are exclusively breastfeeding (providing no formula or solid food), you may start the medication six weeks postpartum. If you are partially breastfeeding, you should begin the medication three weeks after delivery. Before starting this medication, request and carefully review the manufacturer's patient information leaflet from your doctor or pharmacist. This medication may also be prescribed for purposes other than contraception. If you have questions about alternative uses, consult your healthcare provider. Before starting progestin-only oral contraceptives, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you have any allergies to progestins, aspirin, tartrazine (a yellow dye), or other medications. Provide a complete list of all prescription and nonprescription drugs, vitamins, supplements, and herbal products you are taking, as some medications—such as carbamazepine, phenobarbital, phenytoin, and rifampin—may interact with progestin-only contraceptives. Your doctor may need to adjust your medication dosages or monitor you for side effects. Additionally, disclose if you have a history of breast lumps, breast cancer, abnormal vaginal bleeding, liver disease, liver tumors, or diabetes. Notify your doctor if you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or if you become pregnant while taking this medication. Smoking while using progestin-only contraceptives is strongly discouraged, as it increases the risk of cardiovascular events such as heart attacks and strokes. Unless otherwise directed by your doctor, you may continue your regular diet while taking this medication. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. Then, continue taking the pills at your usual time. If the missed dose is more than three hours late, use an additional method of contraception for the next 48 hours. Progestin-only oral contraceptives may cause mild side effects, including irregular menstrual periods, headaches, breast tenderness, nausea, dizziness, acne, or increased hair growth. If these symptoms persist or worsen, inform your doctor. Rare but serious side effects include prolonged bleeding, absence of menstrual periods, or severe abdominal pain. Although combined estrogen-progestin contraceptives are associated with an increased risk of breast cancer, endometrial cancer, and liver tumors, it is unclear whether progestin-only contraceptives carry the same risks. Discuss these potential risks with your doctor. If you experience any unusual or severe side effects, contact your doctor immediately. Serious adverse effects can also be reported to the FDA's MedWatch program. Store this medication in its original container, tightly sealed, and out of reach of children. Keep it at room temperature, away from excessive heat and moisture. Do not store it in the bathroom. Dispose of expired or unused medication properly, and consult your pharmacist for guidance on disposal. In the event of an overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual has collapsed or is not breathing, call emergency services at 911. Keep all scheduled appointments with your doctor. Inform laboratory personnel that you are taking progestin-only contraceptives, as this medication may interfere with certain lab tests. Although rare, pregnancy can occur while taking oral contraceptives. If your period is late, you have missed one or more doses, or you had unprotected sex without backup contraception, take a pregnancy test if it has been more than 45 days since your last period. If you wish to conceive, discontinue the medication. Progestin-only contraceptives should not delay your ability to become pregnant after stopping them. Do not share this medication with others, and consult your pharmacist if you have questions about refills. Brand names for progestin-only oral contraceptives include Micronor®, Nor-Q D®, Ovrette®, and Plan B®. They are also referred to as the minipill and may contain active ingredients such as norethindrone or norgestrel.
